**Kilobot — a thousand robots, three local rules, and twelve hours (2014)**

On 15 August 2014, Michael Rubenstein, Alejandro Cornejo and Radhika Nagpal published programmable self-assembly in a swarm of 1,024 robots (Science 345, 795–799). The hardware is deliberately poor: coin-sized units that shuffle on three stick legs driven by vibrating motors, with infrared to immediate neighbours and no GPS. Four seed robots define the origin of a coordinate system, a target shape is broadcast, and the collective runs on three primitives — gradient formation to learn how far a robot sits from the seed, edge-following to travel around the outside of the group, and localisation by trilateration against neighbours. No robot holds the shape's global state.

What the local rules bought was tolerance of unreliable parts. Rubenstein was blunt about the components: "These robots are much simpler than many conventional robots, and as a result, their abilities are more variable and less reliable." Units struggle to drive straight and their distance sensing varies between them. The algorithm absorbs this by averaging neighbours' distance estimates rather than trusting any one reading, and by having neighbours detect and cooperatively unstick a robot that reports motion while its measured distances refuse to change. In Harvard's account of the run, traffic jams and imprecise positioning were common, and the swarm repaired them with no controller involved.

The bill came due in wall-clock time. Assembling a shape took roughly twelve hours, and adding robots does not fix that: units that have not yet placed themselves queue along the outside of the group and enter one behind another, so contention on the edge, not compute, sets the pace.

The published criticism went at the ceiling rather than the speed. In a 2017 eLetter response to the paper (arXiv 1708.03341), Muaz Niazi argued the system "lacks in terms of matching motility and complex shapes with holes, thereby limiting practical similarity to self-assembly in living systems". And because no robot carries the global picture, whether the shape is finished is a judgement made from outside the swarm.

That last property is the one to carry into a stigmergic agent design. Trading direct messaging for a shared decaying medium buys the resilience on show here: agents fail, the trail is re-laid, the population grows without anyone reconfiguring a topology. It does not buy a termination signal, and it does not make convergence fast. Before you replace an orchestrator with a pheromone store, decide what is allowed to declare the work done, and measure how long your swarm takes to settle — neither answer will come from inside it.

**FCC incentive auction — the mechanism whose incentive guarantee ran on a SAT solver (2016–2017)**

The US broadcast incentive auction bought spectrum back from television stations in a reverse auction and resold it to carriers in a forward auction, both closing on 30 March 2017. The Congressional Research Service records the outcome: $19.8 billion gross from the forward auction, $10.05 billion paid out to 175 winning stations, more than $7.3 billion to the Treasury, and 84 MHz repurposed. Real money, moving on the strength of a mechanism design.

The textbook answer here is Vickrey, and the designers did not use it. Paul Milgrom and Ilya Segal built a descending-clock reverse auction of the deferred-acceptance family. A station is repeatedly asked one question — will you keep broadcasting at this lower price, or exit? — and its price only falls if the auction can still fit it somewhere. Deferred-acceptance auctions with threshold pricing are weakly group-strategyproof and implementable as a clock, properties VCG does not have, and a clock never has to collect or publish a losing bid at all.

The reason a sealed-bid mechanism was unattractive is the winner-determination step. Deciding whether a set of stations can share the remaining channels without interference is graph colouring wearing a hat — NP-complete — and the auction had to answer it afresh before nearly every price decrement. The FCC's solver, SATFC, was built by Neil Newman, Alexandre Fréchette and Kevin Leyton-Brown as a portfolio of eight parallel algorithms with heavy caching, and it solved more than 95% of the problems it met inside the time it was allowed.

That 95% is where the economics and the code fuse. If the checker cannot prove within its deadline that a station is still packable, the auction cannot lower that station's price, and the station stays in and gets paid. Simulating the design, Newman, Leyton-Brown, Milgrom and Segal found the reverse clock auction reaches very efficient allocations, that the FCC's scoring rule greatly reduces total payments to broadcasters at the cost of some efficiency, and that a poor feasibility checker has grave consequences for both the auction's cost and its efficiency (arXiv 1706.04324). A timeout is not a latency incident here. It is a transfer of public money.

When you stand up the Vickrey task auction in this lesson, the incentive-compatibility proof covers the pricing rule and nothing else. Your winner determination is code with a deadline, and whatever it does when that deadline expires — shed late bids, fall back to greedy, award to the first acceptable bidder — is part of the mechanism your agents optimise against. Specify that fallback as carefully as the payment rule, because it is the one they will learn to trigger.

**CME Group — five seconds of nothing stopped a loop nobody had designed (2010)**

The joint CFTC–SEC report into the events of 6 May 2010, published on 30 September that year, is the best-documented case of emergent coordination going wrong between automated agents that had never been introduced to each other. It began with an ordinary instruction. A mutual fund complex told an execution algorithm to sell 75,000 E-Mini S&P 500 futures contracts, around $4.1 billion of notional, and configured it to feed orders at 9% of the trailing minute's trading volume, with no price limit and no time limit. It finished in roughly twenty minutes; a block that size would ordinarily take five hours or more.

The interesting mechanism is the coupling, not the order. High-frequency participants absorbed the selling, then, unwilling to carry the inventory, passed the contracts to one another. Every round trip printed as volume. The seller's feed rate was a function of volume. So the machines recycling contracts between themselves told the execution algorithm the market had got deeper, and it answered by selling faster, which produced more recycling. Neither side could see the loop: each agent behaved exactly to specification, and no participant held a model of the aggregate.

The report puts a number on how hollow that volume was. Between 2:45:13 and 2:45:27 p.m., high-frequency traders traded over 27,000 contracts — about 49 percent of total trading volume in that window — while buying only about 200 additional contracts net. Fourteen seconds, half the market's apparent activity, almost no change in anyone's position. Every per-agent dashboard would have looked healthy.

What broke the loop was not a smarter agent. At 2:45:28 p.m. the CME's Globex Stop Logic Functionality fired and paused E-Mini trading for five seconds — a pre-trade safeguard that halts matching when resting orders are too thin to absorb a cascade. Five seconds of nothing was enough to break the coupling, and prices began to recover. The regulator that mattered was crude, exchange-level and indifferent to who was trading.

This lesson names four conditions for emergence, and the fourth — negative feedback — is the one teams skip, because it reads as giving up capability already paid for. The lesson from this event is where the brake belongs. Per-agent rate limits would have changed nothing: no individual agent misbehaved, and the loop lived in the coupling between them. If your swarm has agents whose activity feeds a signal other agents read — a pheromone store, a reputation score, a queue-depth metric used for routing — you need a population-level circuit breaker that can halt the medium itself, and an aggregate observable that would have shown someone volume rising while net progress was not.

**Discord — when the fan-out had to stop going through one process (2017)**

Discord's write-up on reaching 5,000,000 concurrent users is candid about where a message-passing architecture stops scaling. The shape will be familiar: a session process per connected client, a guild process per server, and a publish that fans out from the guild to every session attached to it. That works until a guild gets large. The r/Overwatch community reached 30,000 concurrent users in a single guild, and the fan-out was a loop in one process.

The measurement makes this worth reading. A single `send/2` between Erlang processes cost 30μs to 70μs of wall clock, mostly from de-scheduling — small enough to ignore anywhere else. Multiplied by 30,000 recipients, publishing one event to that guild took 900ms to 2.1s. The constraint underneath was structural, and the team stated it plainly: "Erlang processes are effectively single threaded, and the only way to parallelize the work is to shard them." No amount of extra hardware helps when the bottleneck is a per-recipient loop inside one scheduler slot.

The fix was a topology change, not an optimisation. Manifold made the guild group recipient PIDs by remote node and send once per node, to a partitioner there, which consistent-hashes the PIDs across cores and hands them to child workers for delivery. The guild's cost became proportional to the number of machines rather than the number of subscribers. The fan-out was not removed — it was relocated onto hardware that could do it concurrently, at the price of a new process in the delivery path of every message.

The second failure generalises further. Five million sessions were served by ten guild registry processes. Under load, requests to those processes timed out; clients retried; retries queued behind requests that had already expired. In Discord's words, the system would "perpetually pile up requests and get into an unrecoverable state", ending in out-of-memory crashes. The remedy, Semaphore, uses atomic ETS counters to refuse work at a shared coordination point instead of accepting it into a mailbox — reject early rather than queue. A companion fix cut a hot hash-ring lookup from around 12μs to 0.3μs so reconnect storms did not re-create the pile-up.

Both failures map onto the tiered router in this lesson, and neither shows up in a load test that ramps one dimension. Check whether any coordinator does per-agent work in a single-threaded loop, and make that cost scale with shard count rather than agent count. Then look at the dispatcher's behaviour at the shed threshold: if it queues rather than refuses, and your agents retry on timeout, you have not built back-pressure — you have built an amplifier, and it will fire on the day a recovery brings every agent back at once.

**SWIFT — the federation authenticated the message, not the building it came from (2016)**

SWIFT is a member-owned cooperative running the closest thing global finance has to a federation protocol: agreed message formats, a central network, and a gateway each member runs inside its own perimeter. Its trust model is the default most cross-organisation designs reach for — the network verifies a message came from a member, and what happens on the member's side of the wire is the member's business.

In February 2016 attackers inside Bangladesh Bank's network used that gateway to issue 35 payment orders worth about $951 million against its account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. BAE Systems Applied Intelligence later documented malware written for the bank's SWIFT client, which suppressed confirmations and altered local records so the payments left no local trace. Thirty orders, some $850 million, were blocked. About $101 million went: $81 million to Rizal Commercial Banking Corporation in Manila and $20 million to Sri Lanka. The Sri Lankan leg failed because the beneficiary, the Shalika Foundation, was typed as "Shalika Fandation", and Deutsche Bank as routing bank queried the spelling.

Every one of those instructions was validly authenticated; the New York Fed executed correctly credentialed orders from a trusted member, which is what the protocol asked of it. Trust had been granted at the granularity of "is this a member" rather than "is this member's environment still sound today", and nothing in the federation answered the second question. The control that caught money in flight was a human reading a beneficiary name.

Liability did not land on the network. SWIFT's model is explicitly shared: it secures the central infrastructure, and each user is accountable for the local systems it runs to connect and transact. So the fight went to the parties: Bangladesh Bank pursued RCBC in the New York courts, and the Philippine central bank fined RCBC nearly $52.92 million. What changed centrally was the membership bargain: SWIFT's Customer Security Programme, launched in 2016, set out eight principles with 16 mandatory and 11 advisory controls, and requires every user to self-attest against the mandatory set through a registry counterparties can read.

The trust store in this lesson records what a partner may do: a capability, a level, a data classification, an expiry. None records whether the partner's environment is still worth trusting this quarter, and a signature from a breached partner satisfies all of them. Settle the equivalent before your first cross-organisation call: what a partner must re-prove and how often, who may read that posture, and which party absorbs the loss when a correctly signed request came from a partner already breached.
